summary: AstroSearchX is a public web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into a searchable time-lapse of the sky. Pick any patch of sky on an interactive map and the tool plays SPHEREx images of that patch across every survey pass, so moving and variable objects stand out. Behind the website, an automatic survey crawler works outward from the North Ecliptic Pole, detects sources in each frame, measures their motion, and cross-checks every detection against Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, 2MASS, SIMBAD, and JPL asteroid data. Anything that moves and matches nothing known is kept and labeled a candidate, never a discovery. The goal is to help find the solar system's faintest and missing members, from brown dwarfs to a possible Planet X, in data anyone can explore.
details:
What it does: AstroSearchX lets anyone explore NASA's SPHEREx survey as a time-lapse. On the website, built on an Aladin Lite sky map, you search by coordinates or object name, pick a patch of sky, choose a field of view and wavelength band, and play SPHEREx frames from every pass as a blink comparison, a stack, or a difference view. Pressing "Find what moves" runs the detection engine on that patch.

How it works: the backend pulls SPHEREx cutouts from the IRSA archive (the DR1 and Quick Release 3 collections), aligns them to sub-pixel accuracy, detects sources in each frame, links them across frames, and fits each object's motion. It keeps only motion larger than the measurement error, flags brightness changes, and masks artifacts using SPHEREx quality flags. Every detection is then verified against Gaia DR3 proper motions projected to each frame's date, CatWISE2020, 2MASS, SIMBAD, and SkyBoT and JPL SBIdent for known asteroids. Each object is classified as a known moving star, a known asteroid or comet, a variable star, an artifact, or an unknown candidate. On-the-fly spectra flag methane and water absorption, a sign of a cool brown dwarf, and every candidate carries a reliability verdict.

The survey: an offline crawler surveys the sky on its own, starting at the North Ecliptic Pole, where SPHEREx revisits most often, and spiraling outward over HEALPix patches. It saves its progress and resumes after restarts, and it can re-run when new SPHEREx data is released.

Results so far: the engine measured Barnard's Star at 10.45 arcsec per year, matching Gaia to about 0.2 pixels, and Epsilon Indi B at 4.65 arcsec per year at 31 sigma with a fitted parallax of 0.36 arcsec. The faint brown dwarf WISE 0855 appears in stacked passes at 7.05 plus or minus 1.35 arcsec per year. In a validation run over 15 fields and 7,581 objects, zero of 5,701 Gaia-static stars were falsely reported as movers.

Tools: Python 3.12 with FastAPI, astropy, astroquery, pyvo, reproject, and photutils on the backend; React, Vite, Aladin Lite, and Plotly.js in the browser; SQLite for the survey queue; the backend runs on Render and the site on GitHub Pages. Full code: https://github.com/Ronith-Neelam1429/MongooseInSpace_SPHEREx-PlanetX

Why it matters: SPHEREx images the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, far more data than anyone can inspect by eye. AstroSearchX makes that data explorable by anyone and does the first pass of the search automatically, so real candidates surface faster and false alarms get filtered out with catalog evidence, not guesses.
